title: The one whose head He guards
hook: the one who has You over his head, how can he suffer (Suhi M5, ang 749)

segments.voice: Yesterday, baani, and your line: as the word comes. What true thing did you say? Speaking that plainly takes courage. Today, where Guru Arjan says that courage comes from. Day six hundred sixty.

In Punjabi homes, when a child bends to touch a grandparent's feet, the grandparent often does one thing without thinking: they rest a hand on the child's head. A second, maybe two. It means: I bless you, I've got you, you're under my care. There's even an everyday phrase for having someone's hand on your head, meaning you have a protector, someone who stands behind you. Guru Arjan took that gesture and lifted it as high as it can go.
screen: `A CHILD TOUCHES AN ELDER'S FEET.` → `A HAND RESTS ON THE HEAD.` → `I'VE GOT YOU.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Suhi, on ang 749. It begins, in effect: the one over whose head You stand, my Master, how could such a one suffer? Then it turns to the opposite person: someone drunk on the world's glitter doesn't know how to speak, and never remembers that he will die. Then the refrain: my Sovereign, You belong to Your devoted ones, and they belong to You. Your servant has no fear; even death's messenger doesn't come near. The word in the first line is sir, head. And in the gesture, as in the hymn, the head is where blessing lands and where protection is felt. Now, the honest question, the same one we asked about You are my father. Does this mean nothing bad ever happens to the faithful? Guru Arjan himself answers that, with his life. In 1606 he was arrested by the Mughal authorities in Lahore and died in their custody, after suffering Sikhs remember with grief every year. He's honored as the first Sikh martyr. So the hymn can't mean his devoted ones never meet pain. Sikhs read it at a deeper level: the one under the Master's hand isn't crushed by suffering. Dukh, pain, can come, but it doesn't own them. The fear is gone, even when the danger isn't. Tradition remembers Guru Arjan in his last days repeating that the Lord's will is sweet. That's what a guarded head looks like: not a life without storms, but a person who stays steady inside one.
screen: `SIR: THE HEAD, WHERE BLESSING LANDS.` · `HOW COULD SUCH A ONE SUFFER?` · `GURU ARJAN, MARTYRED IN 1606.` · `PAIN COMES, BUT DOESN'T OWN THEM.` · then, large: `GUARDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest your hand on your head. Gently, the way a grandparent would. Feel its weight, its warmth. Let your shoulders drop under it. Think of who has been that hand for you: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend. And if you pray, let it stand for the One's hand, and say Waheguru quietly. Then think of something you're afraid of right now. Hold the fear and the hand at the same time. Notice which one feels bigger. When you're ready, lower your hand and rest. The bell holds the time.
Sir, head, where blessing lands: Guru Arjan says the one with the Master's hand over it may meet pain, but not fear.
Your line: guarded. Today, when fear rises, touch the top of your head for a second and say the word. Day six hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Suhi shabad 'jis ke sir oopar toon suaamee' in kirtan, especially in hard times, and remember his martyrdom in 1606 each year.

fork.setup: Guru Arjan wrote that the one under the Master's hand cannot suffer. then he was arrested and tortured. what does tradition remember him saying?

fork.reveal: pain came, but did not own him: a guarded head is a steady one, not a sheltered one.

original.note: Gurmukhi: head; jis ke sir oopar, the one over whose head You stand.

trapdoor: what you thought: God protects good people from bad things.
what it means: the one under the Master's hand isn't owned by pain or fear, even when hardship comes.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's own martyrdom in 1606 is the lens Sikhs use for this shabad; the image draws on the Punjabi gesture and idiom of an elder's hand on the head.
